# Implement block: Slingshot Send Money (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Slingshot Send Money" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A full-screen send-money confirmation with no cards: a vertical sheet of satin bands (dusty rose at the top, near-black brown behind the amount, a mauve band under the hint, red-brown at the bottom), the recipient's round picture with the initial "D" and the name "Dave" at the top, "$4.50" in white 64 pt bold at 37% of the height, the hint "SWIPE DOWN" in wide-spaced capitals at 58%, and a round close and a round pencil button in the bottom corners. Dragging down anywhere pulls the amount like the pouch of a slingshot: it trails the finger with ghost copies smearing behind it and leans as if it hung from the recipient, the hint follows less far, the bands stretch down and the top two thirds of the screen heat to amber in proportion to the pull; past the threshold the hint reads "RELEASE TO SEND" and the corner buttons fade out. Letting go there fires the amount up into the recipient, shrinking and fading with its ghosts behind it while the amber drains; a green disc with a white check then pops in where the amount was, with "Sent" under it and a "Done" pill rising from the bottom, and Done drops the amount back out of the picture. Letting go short of the threshold springs everything back.

**Motion.** Nothing is tied to the finger. A drag of (dx, dy) sets an aim: down by 0.8 × dy up to 24.5% of the screen's height, then with rubber-band resistance (at most 56 pt more), and sideways by 0.32 × dx (±46 pt). The amount is drawn four times, each copy chasing the aim on its own spring (mass 1; stiffness/damping 170/16 for the text, 118/13.5, 84/11.5 and 60/10 for its ghosts at 36%, 24% and 14% opacity); a ghost shows in proportion to how far it trails the aim, fully at 22 pt, so resting text is sharp and moving text smears. A copy that lags is strained: up to 24% taller and 7% narrower at 150 pt behind. Each copy is rotated by −x/420 rad. The hint has the same four copies on softer springs (110/14, 80/12, 58/10.5, 42/9) and travels 62% as far. Heat is the pull as a share of the travel on a spring (130/20): it mixes the 14 gradient colours from the satin palette to the amber one, moves their stops down, and fades in a radial amber glow (30%) under the recipient; the corner buttons fade out between 45% and 80% heat. At 72% of the travel the pull is armed: the hint's wordings cross-fade in 140 ms (white 60% to 90%) with a medium haptic, a light one when it falls back. Release when armed: the aim jumps to the recipient's picture, so the copies fly up on the same springs (about 0.25 s), shrinking to 40% and fading out between 30% and 72% of the way; the hint fades in 220 ms as it rises; the picture swells 10% at 150 ms (90 ms in, spring 260/12 out). 900 ms after the release the check disc pops from scale 0 (spring 260/15), the recipient fades out in 250 ms, the Done pill rises from below the screen (spring 190/19), and 120 ms later the check stroke draws in 220 ms as "Sent" fades in, with a success haptic. Done: check and label fade in 180 ms, the pill sinks in 260 ms (cubic ease-in), the recipient fades in over 250 ms, the amount springs back down from the picture with its ghosts, the corner buttons return after 260 ms and the hint after 320 ms over 350 ms. A release that is not armed puts the aim back to zero and the springs carry everything home with a small overshoot. The self-playing demo moves the same aim from a clock, period 9 s: a test pull to 42% from 0.8 s (0.5 s cubic ease-out) released at 1.45 s, a full pull from 2.3 s over 0.95 s (smoothstep) drifting 34 pt to the right, a hold in which the finger trembles by 2% (9 rad/s) and wanders to 34 pt left, the release at 4.3 s, Done pressed at 7.0 s for 150 ms, then rest; it gives no haptics, and a touch stops it until 3 s after the last touch, when it starts again from rest. Under reduced motion the springs jump (no lag, no ghosts, no strain), the amount fades out where it was let go instead of flying, and the check and the pill fade in instead of popping and rising. Jetpack Compose uses a layered avatar-shadow approximation on Android 26–27. Manual pan translation follows the React Native platform behavior: iOS keeps the default pan translation, while Android resets its translation origin at activation.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [SlingshotSendMoneyDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/SlingshotSendMoney/SlingshotSendMoneyDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [SlingshotSendMoney.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Forms/SlingshotSendMoney/SlingshotSendMoney.swift)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
